content.text: Middleware and endpoint filters both wrap code around a request, but they sit in different places. Middleware runs for every request, before and around routing, and sees only the raw

. An endpoint filter runs only for the endpoints it's attached to, after their arguments are bound, and sees those typed arguments and the handler's result. Keep app-wide plumbing in middleware and put rules about specific endpoints in filters.
An orders API has a rule: customers can only place orders for themselves. A middleware enforces it. For
, it reads the JSON body, compares its
with the caller's claim, and answers 403 on a mismatch. Months later, a security review finds that
accepts any customer id, and so does
with a trailing slash. Both requests reach real endpoints. Neither matches the string the middleware compares against, so the check never runs, and nothing fails to tell anyone.
The belief: middleware and endpoint filters are two syntaxes for the same idea, so all
logic can live in middleware. One place, runs for everything, nothing to forget.
It's a reasonable belief. Both have the same shape: a

delegate, code before and after it, and an early return that skips the rest. The docs even describe filter order with the same nesting picture as the pipeline. Middleware is also the older tool: minimal APIs got endpoint filters only in .NET 7, so a lot of existing code does everything in middleware. And a path check or
seems to make any middleware endpoint-specific.
What the belief skips is where each one runs and what exists at that moment. That difference decides what each one can check reliably.

chain first. Routing picks an endpoint, more middleware runs, and then the endpoint executes. Inside the endpoint, the framework binds the handler's parameters, runs the filter pipeline (group filters, then the endpoint's own), calls the handler, and passes its return value back out through the filters before writing the response. Middleware is outside the endpoint; an
is inside it. In a test, a filter on the route group ran first, then the endpoint's filter, then the handler.

: headers, the user, and, after routing, the route values and the endpoint's metadata. The body is only a stream. To inspect it, you enable buffering, deserialize it, rewind it, and let the endpoint deserialize it again. On the way out, the response is already bytes.
: the handler's arguments, already bound by
and in declaration order, which it can read or replace. After
, it gets the handler's return value as an object, before serialization, and can return something else.

Middleware runs for every request that reaches it: static files, health checks, CORS preflights, URLs that match no endpoint. To target specific endpoints, it has to recognize URLs, and that's where the hook went wrong. Routing treated
A filter is attached to an endpoint or a route group, so it follows the endpoint whatever its URL. A filter on a group runs for every endpoint in it, including endpoints added to the group later.

Filters run only once an endpoint is chosen, so 404s never reach them. They also don't run when reading the body fails, such as malformed JSON or an unsupported content type: the framework answers 400 first. Other binding failures, like a route value that doesn't parse, do run the filters, with the status code already set to 400 and the handler skipped.

How to apply it in your project
. Each check that targets specific endpoints is a candidate for a filter, or for endpoint metadata.
Exception handling, HTTPS redirection, CORS, authentication, compression and request logging that must include 404s and malformed requests belong in the pipeline.
Put filters on the route group so new endpoints inherit them, and describe what they check with an interface on the request types, so one filter serves many handlers.

items.title: Test the shapes, not just the happy path

content.text: Send the trailing-slash URL, the other verbs, a malformed body and a missing route value through the real app, and assert on the status code each one gets.

items.text: Middleware wraps the whole app; an endpoint filter wraps one endpoint, or one group, after binding.
Filters see typed arguments and the handler's result; middleware sees raw requests and response bytes.
URL checks in middleware drift from routing; a filter on a group follows its endpoints, including new ones.
404s and unreadable bodies never reach filters, so logging and error handling stay in middleware.
